note: Questions raised by the team during design review, NOT PRD workbook rows. Rendered into docs/37-prd-open-questions.md by scripts/build_prd_registers.py so both kinds of question live in one register. Evidence for each: docs/41-auth-ten-open-source-evaluation.md. Closing a row here means editing this file, re-running the script, and applying the answer to the owning doc.

questions.question: Identity component wiring: Better Auth has no Go SDK, so the V1 plan assumes a Node identity surface. Options — A: keep Better Auth, run it in the Node tier behind a documented JWT/JWKS contract for Go (one more deployable); B: Better Auth for flows, Go owns session/refresh-token tables and revocation; C: replace with a multi-tenant IdP (Zitadel AGPL-3.0, or Keycloak if deep SAML/LDAP is needed), everything OIDC; D: build the identity domain in Go (~3-4 dev-weeks, zero extra runtime, BVR-14 superseded). See docs/41 §7.
questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-19 — option C, product P1: ZITADEL** (self-hosted, AGPL-3.0, one instance, Organization per tenant). Better Auth (BVR-14) and Cerbos (BVR-23) are superseded by ADR-13/ADR-14. See docs/41 §10.

questions.question: Does any tenant need SAML/OIDC SSO or SCIM at V1 cutover? Restates PRD row *Auth & Identity #6* as a build decision. The PRD schedules AUTH-24/25 at V3 and every OSS IdP that ships them at V1 (Zitadel, Keycloak, authentik) costs a second identity store plus, for Zitadel, an AGPL-3.0 review. Answering yes promotes AUTH-24/25 into V1 and changes D1.
questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-19 — yes:** one V1 tenant requires SSO at cutover. AUTH-24 (SAML/OIDC federation) is promoted into V1.0/V1.1 scope and AUTH-25 (SCIM) is promoted with it per P3. Recorded as a post-PRD design decision (docs/41 §10), not a PRD workbook row.

questions.question: Isolation enforcement depth: keep ADR-1 app-level only (Go tenant guard + sqlc + CI guard test), or add Postgres RLS as a fail-closed second layer? RLS costs 2-4% on indexed queries and requires transaction-scoped `set_config('app.tenant_id', …, true)` under PgBouncer, `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` and a (tenant_id, …) index on every policy table; a missed guard currently leaks all tenants' rows, with RLS it returns zero rows. See docs/41 §5.
questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-19 — yes: Postgres RLS is adopted** as the fail-closed second enforcement layer on every tenant-owned table (docs/01 §7.8, docs/03 §10). App-level guard (ADR-1) stays.

questions.question: Authorization engine and deployment mode: keep Cerbos (BVR-23) as sidecar/central service, embed the Cerbos Go engine in-process (no extra process, fail-closed hazard disappears), switch to Casbin embedded (Apache-2.0, RBAC-with-domains, fastest, weakest decision logs), or fall back to the in-house engine behind `authorizer.Check`. The docs/02 §11 rule 'PDP unreachable → deny' only applies to the sidecar mode.
questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-19 — Casbin, embedded** in the Go api, RBAC-with-domains model. Cerbos is superseded (ADR-14); the `authorizer.Check` interface is unchanged. See docs/41 §10.

questions.question: Staff 2FA scope in V1: AUTH-09 as written (mandatory for every staff role) or finance + risk only? This is PRD open question 'Auth & Identity #1' restated as a build decision; it sizes the enrolment UX, recovery flow and support load for launch.
questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-19 — all staff roles, enforced at first login, with backup codes in V1**: AUTH-11 (backup codes) is promoted with AUTH-09; AUTH-29 (email change) and AUTH-28 (admin-assisted 2FA reset) become explicit V1 dependencies of the forced-enrolment path.

questions.question: Which identity provider do we adopt (D1 = option C)?
questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-19 — ZITADEL**, self-hosted single instance + Postgres (AGPL-3.0, unmodified). Keycloak rejected on ops weight (1-2 GB, Java) and organisation fit; authentik rejected on hardening track record for fund-holding accounts. Legal review of AGPL obligations is a Phase-0 gate; policy: never patch ZITADEL source, contribute upstream.

questions.question: Where do the login page and session live (D1 = C)?
questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-19 — IdP-hosted login + IdP tokens at the API.** Users log in on ZITADEL Hosted Login v2 (org-scoped via `urn:zitadel:iam:org:id:{id}`), the api accepts the ZITADEL access token and keeps a Redis deny-set + `auth_sessions` projection for immediate revocation (AUTH-07/20/27/39). Our `/v1/auth/login|refresh` contract is retired in favour of OIDC endpoints; `contracts/api/auth.md` and `contracts/shared/openapi.yaml` are updated accordingly.

questions.question: With SSO needed at cutover, how far does SSO/SCIM go in V1 (D2 = yes)?
questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-19 — SSO + SCIM for that tenant.** AUTH-24 and AUTH-25 both promoted into V1. ZITADEL limits SCIM to the User schema (no Groups, verified 2026-09-19), so deprovisioning is user-level; role assignment stays with us (P4) and group-to-role mapping is out of scope for the SCIM path.

questions.question: Roles and membership: which system owns them (AUTH-12/13/14, TEN-32)?
questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-19 — our Postgres is authoritative** for tenant membership, roles, custom roles and the `resource.action` permission registry. ZITADEL organizations are used for login scoping, per-org policies and SSO routing; ZITADEL user grants mirror our roles only so tokens can carry them (Actions v2 `preAccessToken`), and a reconciliation job reports drift (TEN-32 access review).

questions.question: Per-identity concurrent session limit (AUTH-07): the contracts/api/auth.md open item. How many active sessions may one identity hold at once, and what happens on overflow?
questions.answer: **Open — default recorded:** 10 concurrent sessions per identity, oldest evicted (the newest login wins and the evicted session gets `auth.session_revoked` plus a `user.session_revoked` event with reason `concurrency_limit`). Raise only if trader feedback demands it; the running count lives in `auth_sessions` and is checked at `/v1/auth/session` time.

questions.question: TTS cutover password posture (docs/25 §3.5, AUTH-01/05/17): import existing password hashes into ZITADEL (traders keep passwords) or force a reset at first login?
questions.answer: **Open — default recorded:** force reset (`passwordChangeRequired=true`, the docs/25 §3.5 posture B). Import-and-keep is technically available since ZITADEL accepts hashed passwords when the source algorithm is enabled in the password-hasher verifier list (verified 2026-09-19, review G9); the COO can switch to posture A at the gate if TTS supplies verified per-user hashes with a supported KDF.

questions.question: Tenant login hostname (docs/03 §3.8, TEN-05): does the tenant's own domain ever serve the login page in V1?
questions.answer: **Open — default recorded:** no. V1 logins happen on `login.alpha1.io` scoped to the tenant organization (per-org branding, policies and MFA settings); tenant domains serve the app and the API only, with a silent OIDC redirect back to the tenant host after login. The vanity login host (`login.firm.com`, edge rewrite preserving the org scope) ships with TEN-05 in V2 if tenants ask.

questions.question: GDPR erasure across two stores (docs/02 §10.4, AUTH-35): ZITADEL is event-sourced and does not de-identify past events (upstream issue #7811, open). Is the residual PII (email + display name in the IdP event stream) acceptable, or do we need a compensating control?
questions.answer: **Open — default recorded:** accept and document. We store no more PII in the IdP than email + display name (KYC profile and documents stay in our stores), the erasure procedure deletes the user and our rows, and the residual event entries are recorded as a known limitation with a DPO review at Phase 0 exit. Compensating control if the DPO refuses: pseudo-anonymous login names (`usr_{ulid}@login.alpha1.io`) with the notification email held only in our database.

questions.question: Access/refresh token lifetimes and rotation (restates the open PRD workbook question as a build decision): ZITADEL's instance default is 12 h access tokens, so the 15-min figure in docs/02 §3.2 is documented but not enforced — what do we set, and where?
questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-19 — access/ID 15 min, refresh idle 30 min, absolute 30 d, rotation on every use with reuse detection.** Written at provisioning through the instance OIDC-settings endpoint (`/admin/v1/settings/oidc`, update = method `PUT`, all four fields required, seconds precision) and read back at Phase 0 (docs/99 gate 6). This is the bound that holds when the deprovisioning pipeline *and* its alerting are both down (docs/43 §6).

questions.question: How does an IdP-side deprovisioning (tenant SCIM deactivation, ZITADEL-console user removal, or user self-deletion) reach `tenant_memberships` before anyone notices — given that nightly reconciliation does not exist yet and Actions v2 event executions have no retry?
questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-19 — a pull consumer (`idp-sync`), not a webhook.** The worker polls ZITADEL's event log (`admin/v1/events/_search`, sequence cursor, 10 s) through a durable inbox and applies the AUTH-20 suspension path; covered event types, retry/DLQ/alerting and the nightly direction-aware reconciliation (safety net, never the mechanism) are specified in docs/43 §3–§7. Actions v2 event executions are rejected as the transport: no retry (upstream #10268) and instance-breaking event conditions (upstream #12225).

questions.question: Self-service account deletion: ZITADEL lets a user irreversibly delete their own account (`user.self.delete`, reached via `ORG_USER_SELF_MANAGER` / `SELF_MANAGEMENT_GLOBAL`, from the console or the API). Do we grant it in V1 and accept that nothing in our stack can intercept it?
questions.answer: **Open — default recorded:** no self-delete-capable role grants in V1 and no self-service delete surface; closure runs through staff (V1 runbook → V2 `AUTH-35` flow) with business checks, a payout hold and the actor recorded as `system:account-closure`. Enforced by detection: an alert on `user.grant.added` containing `ORG_USER_SELF_MANAGER` and on `instance.member.added` containing `SELF_MANAGEMENT_GLOBAL`. The cost — no self-service erasure until V2 — is the DPO's call at gate 8 (docs/43 §8); the `defaults.yaml` role-permission override is a recorded Phase-0 option, not a default.

questions.question: One person can hold one ZITADEL user per organization, but `identities` carried a single `idp_user_id` — a trader registering at a second tenant overwrites the first org's pointer, and that org's deprovisioning events (`user.deactivated` / `user.removed`) then resolve to no identity and land in the DLQ. What is the identity↔IdP join model?
questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-19 — `identity_idp_links` (one row per identity×org).** New table `identity_idp_links(idp_user_id PK, identity_id, idp_org_id, tenant_id NULL = platform, state active|retired, first/last_seen, retired_at)`, `UNIQUE(identity_id, idp_org_id)`; `identities.idp_user_id`/`idp_org_id` demoted to a "last used" pointer. Login resolves link → `identity_key` fallback; `idp-sync` maps `aggregate_id` through links and holds the cursor plus alerts on an unknown link (never guesses a tenant); a deleted user's link is retired and stays as the audit alias (docs/43 §9). Written into docs/02 §3.1/§3.2/§9 and docs/43 §3/§4.

questions.question: No role→permission-key binding existed for the 31-key registry and the tenant/platform role sets, so `authorizer.Check` had no policy to evaluate; the registry carried four decision-shaped TODOs (sensitive-data key per AUD-23, `audit.read`/`analytics.read` naming, trader self-actions, `payout.read_queue` masking). Derive and ratify now, or defer?
questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-19 — derive and ratify now.** `contracts/permissions/roles.yaml` is the machine-readable source (12 roles in two realms, `scope` all/own/platform, effective holder sets closed under descendants, ABAC constraints recorded per key); it seeds the `casbin_rule` migration and `scripts/verify_roles.py` keeps YAML ⇄ seed ⇄ docs/02 §3.1 identical. TODOs closed: sensitive-data access = `kyc.document.read` + `payout.method.review` (audit-on-access, AUD-23); names ratified (`payout.read_queue` keeps its name); trader self-actions = declared keys with scope `own`; three platform keys promoted to V1 (`platform.identity.admin`, `platform.tenant.provision`, `platform.session.revoke`) and one reserved (`platform.analytics.read`). Platform role catalogs unified (`platform:super_admin` supersedes `platform:owner`/`admin`/`billing`). Registry now 36 V1 keys.

questions.question: Casbin storage, reload, change-audit and boot behaviour were unspecified (ADR-14 said "rows in Postgres"; no DDL existed anywhere): where do the policies live, how do the api instances learn about a change, and what happens if the policy set cannot be loaded?
questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-19 — `casbin_rule` + versioning + Redis reload + fail closed.** The policy table is seeded **by migration** from `roles.yaml` (V1 has no policy-CRUD surface); every change bumps `authz_policy_versions`, writes an `audit_events` row, and publishes `casbin:reload` on Redis, with a ≤ 30 s version re-check so a missed message self-heals; an empty or unloadable policy set at boot denies everything and raises a SEV-1 alert — never allow. DDL and the change lifecycle are in docs/02 §9 (ADR-14 amended).

questions.question: Fail-closed RLS (D3) has no exemption model: cross-tenant readers (relay, ledger/audit appliers, ANA, CON, `idp-sync`), the pre-tenant-context lookups (session by id, API key by hash) and console sessions (`auth_sessions.tenant_id IS NULL`) cannot work under the tenant policy as written, and migrations run under `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`. What is the exemption model?
questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-19 — one named platform role, enumerated, with accessors for pre-auth reads.** `app_platform` holds `BYPASSRLS` and is used **only** by the enumerated cross-tenant services, whose queries must still carry explicit `tenant_id` predicates (CI grep-class check + review — RLS is their backstop, not their isolation); `app_rw` stays fail-closed; `migrator` is a discrete DDL job. The four context-free reads go through `SECURITY DEFINER` accessors in the `auth` schema (session by id, API key by hash, link by `idp_user_id`, console-session check); the platform-owned tables are listed explicitly so "every policy table" cannot be read as "all tables". docs/02 §9 + docs/28 §3.3.

questions.question: P2 chose "IdP-issued tokens, no own rotating-refresh stack", but docs/02 §3.2 implemented rotation/reuse detection ourselves and the schema carried `refresh_hash` / `prev_refresh_hash`. Who owns refresh rotation and reuse detection?
questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-19 — ZITADEL owns rotation and reuse detection; we own the response.** The `refresh_hash` / `prev_refresh_hash` columns and our reuse-detection logic are removed; a reused token revokes its family in the IdP, and our side keeps the Redis deny-set, `auth_sessions` projection, `RevokeAllMyRefreshTokens` + `DeleteSession` kill and the CRITICAL audit. One owner per concern, no second refresh state to reconcile.

questions.question: V1 API-key surface was contradictory: docs/02 §3.5 and blueprint step 7 build the primitives, while the GW chain, `contracts/api/auth.md` and the endpoint table all say keys are V2 with no endpoint. Which is it?
questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-19 — primitives only, internal consumers only.** V1 ships create/revoke/hash/scope helpers for service tokens and the future AUTH-21 surface; there is **no tenant-facing key endpoint** in V1, and the GW chain note now names the internal consumer instead of saying "keys are V2". Tenant machine integrations use TEN-11 integration secrets until AUTH-21 ships.

questions.question: The token did not prove which tenant it was for: `tenants` carried no OIDC client/application binding, docs/02 said "one project + OIDC application" instance-wide while docs/03's saga provisioned a project per org, and a token minted for tenant A was accepted on tenant B's host. Per-tenant audience + session binding, or one shared application with an org claim?
questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-19 — per-tenant application + binding (option A).** One ZITADEL project + OIDC application **per tenant org**; `tenants.idp_client_id` is stored (client secret in the tenant secret store, referenced by `tenants.idp_client_secret_ref`). Every `/session` requires `aud` == that tenant's client id and checks the org claim when present; the `auth_sessions` row is bound to the tenant resolved from the request domain, so a token presented on another tenant's host is refused with the new `auth.tenant_mismatch` (403). Provisioning step 3 writes the binding.

questions.question: `identity_key` was the mutable join key: `AUTH-29` rewrote it on email change, which silently creates a second identity for one person, moves the `AUTH-36` merge anchor and stops the old address resolving. Make the join key immutable with an email table, or keep one mutable key?
questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-19 — immutable key + email table (option A).** `identities.identity_key` = hash of the **first verified email** and never moves. New `identity_emails(identity_id, email_hash UNIQUE, email, is_primary, verified_at, retired_at)` is the match key for `/session`, `idp-sync` and `AUTH-36` merges; an email change adds a row and flips `is_primary`, and the old row is retained so a login on the old address still resolves to the same person (`identities.email` is only a cache).

questions.question: Cross-org auto-link (an existing identity gaining a link in a new org) trusted an undefined "verified email" and had no abuse control — a matching address at a second org silently attached to the existing identity (identity poisoning). What gate applies?
questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-19 — verified-email gate + audited link (option A).** Auto-link requires a verified email (token `email_verified` **and** ZITADEL's user email state = verified). An unverified address creates a **separate identity + merge task** for staff. Every cross-org link writes a **CRITICAL** audit event and notifies the identity's existing org admins; the first org's contact details are never revealed to the second.

questions.question: SSO group→role mapping was contradictory: decision P3 (AUTH-24/25 in V1) implied directory-driven roles, the provisioning saga said "map directory groups → roles", and the registry advertised a viewable map — while the ratified model assigns roles ourselves. And the `invited → active` membership transition was undocumented. Which V1 posture?
questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-19 — no group→role mapping in V1 (option A).** SSO users are assigned roles by us at onboarding (later via platform/ADM actions); directory groups only drive sign-in/provisioning. docs/03 step 3a and the registry `tenant.sso.read` wording are corrected, and the membership lifecycle is documented: `user.human.added`/invite → `invited`, first successful `/v1/auth/session` → `active`.

questions.question: No V1 step-up existed although `payout.approve` requires a factor assertion < 5 min, the taxonomy already had `authz.step_up_required`, and the only planned step-up surface (AUTH-30) is V2. Where does V1 step-up live?
questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-19 — hosted re-auth, server-enforced (option A).** The web tier re-runs hosted login with `prompt=login&max_age=300`; the fresh token carries a new `auth_time` and the `api` enforces the ≤ 5 min freshness rule on the payout keys, returning `authz.step_up_required` (403, `details.max_age`) when stale. The API-owned step-up surface (challenge initiation, AUTH-30) remains V2; V1 has exactly one policy rule and it is enforced server-side, never in the UI.

questions.question: ZITADEL's own admin plane was ungoverned: who holds `IAM_OWNER`, whether the Console/Admin API is reachable from the edge, and what the IdP break-glass is were all unstated — while the authz model assumes the IdP is trusted. What governance applies?
questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-19 — private plane, two owners, quarterly review (option A).** The admin plane (Console, `admin/v1`, `management/v1`) is not reachable from the edge: internal network only, operator access via Cloudflare Access. Exactly **two named `IAM_OWNER` holders** (or one owner plus a sealed emergency credential in the ops vault), both with mandatory MFA (the `alpha1-platform` org is `force_mfa=true`). Every IAM role grant is part of the quarterly access review and is mirrored into our audit stream by `idp-sync` (`instance.member.*`). Runbooks: docs/06 §3.6; first execution is a Phase-0 checklist item (docs/34 §9).

questions.question: Cross-tenant tenant-audit access from the platform realm: docs/05 named a `platform:compliance` role that does not exist in the ratified catalog (G30 closure), while docs/21 CON-01 assigns the console audit view to `platform:super_admin`. Who reads tenant audit cross-tenant (always critical-tier audited)? Options — A: platform:super_admin only (no new role/key); B: new key platform.audit.read bound to super_admin + platform:finance; C: add the platform:compliance role + key. See docs/48 §2.
questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-19 — option A:** `platform:super_admin` only, no new role, no new key. docs/05 §10 corrected to the ratified catalog; a dedicated key can still be proposed at the CON V2 freeze if finance/compliance oversight demands it.

questions.question: The tenant chart of accounts is 'seeded at provisioning' (docs/05 §3.1) but the provisioning saga has no CoA step — the first order.paid post would fail `led.account_not_found`. Options — A: saga step 6b (idempotent, compensated); B: lazy seed inside ledger.Post; C: seed at the go-live checklist. See docs/48 §2.
questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-19 — option A:** the saga gains an idempotent, compensated step 6b (CoA template + platform-account links), documented in docs/03 §3.5 and docs/05 §3.1; the docs/47 saga summary counts 9 steps + 3a + 6b.

questions.question: audit_events.seq was 'app-assigned via Redis INCR' while audit.Write is fail-closed (audit failure = sensitive action denied) and seq has no V1 consumer (the hash chain is V2) — a Redis outage would deny every sensitive action platform-wide. Options — A: drop seq from V1 (V2 chain-init backfills in id order); B: keep seq sourced from Postgres; C: keep Redis INCR and accept the coupling. See docs/48 §2.
questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-19 — option A:** V1 carries no seq; the V2 hash chain (AUD-14) introduces it at chain init, backfilled in id order. The fail-closed audit write is one INSERT in the action's transaction with no Redis dependency.

questions.question: The V1 event catalog has zero EVL/BRG events, yet EVL is Phase-1 V1.0 and the binding machine edge ACTIVE→BREACH_DETECTED (EVL-17) consumes evaluation.verdict — the sheet cannot wire its own core loop. Which events enter the V1 catalog? Options — A: promote the Phase-1 five (evaluation.verdict, bridge.tick, account.day_rolled, account.activated, evaluation.daily_reset); B: promote only the breach-path three; C: keep them out as internal wiring (breaks the EVT-03/AUD-02 mirror + trace for the core loop). See docs/50 §2 F1.
questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-19 — option A:** all five promoted with payload schemas + examples; `bridge.tick` is the observed record (EVL-49) and does not mirror to audit (docs/05 §14 exception).

questions.question: docs/09 §3.7 says an EVL-20 override (V1.1) transitions LCC back 'failed → active', but the binding state machine has no reverse edge out of FAILED and LCC-12's manual override-transition is V2 — a false-positive breach cannot be undone. Options — A: add guarded reversal edges BREACH_DETECTED→ACTIVE and FAILED→ACTIVE (override record = guard); B: reversal only before FAILED commits, post-FAILED is V2; C: never reopen — spawn a replacement account. See docs/50 §2 F2.
questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-19 — option A:** the two edges exist, valid only with a referenced override record (evaluation_overrides.id, kind clear_breach) + step-up; closed positions stay closed; BRG re-enables trading. Machine, diagram source, API contract and docs updated in the same decision.

questions.question: Rule packs include time_limit (max_calendar_days) but the EVL-44 priority matrix never classifies it and the machine has no expiry edge, while account.expired exists with failed_reason 'expired' — what IS a time-limit expiry? Options — A: expiry is a breach verdict (rule_id=time_limit) through the existing breach path; B: a dedicated 'expired' verdict + machine edge + AccountExpired promoted to V1. See docs/50 §2 F3.
questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-19 — option A:** expiry is a breach verdict (matrix priority 1, after max_daily_loss; failed_reason 'breach:time_limit'); account.expired remains the NOT/ANA mirror event. One enforcement path to build and test.

questions.question: LCC freezes trading_time_left while SUSPENDED, but EVL's day_rolled trigger increments calendar_days unconditionally and nothing gates evaluation on account state — a suspended account burns its calendar limit and racks up verdicts while frozen. Options — A: suspension freezes everything (no rollover event, EVL skips suspended ticks, resume re-evaluates on the next fresh tick); B: only the trading clock freezes, evaluation continues. See docs/50 §2 F4.
questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-19 — option A:** the rollover job skips SUSPENDED (and terminal) accounts; EVL skips their ticks with WARN; clocks frozen; V1-Plus pause behaves the same (paused_at). docs/07 §3.3 + docs/09 §3.6/§5 updated.

questions.question: FUNDED accounts have no breach edge: the V1 machine routes FUNDED only to SUSPENDED/TERMINATED, so a breach verdict on a funded account has no automatic transition (docs/50 F13). Options to consider — A: FUNDED→BREACH_DETECTED reusing the breach path (terminates via CLOSING); B: FUNDED→SUSPENDED automatic + risk review decides; C: funded breach = force-terminate path with extra guard. Not decided in the tenth pass.
questions.deadline: Phase 4 wave 3 (trading depth) or first funded-account incident
questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-19 — option A (twelfth pass, docs/52):** FUNDED→BREACH_DETECTED reuses the breach path (evidence, LCC-43 idempotency, CLOSING cleanup); in-flight approved payouts carry the hold flag (status_reason='on_hold', human queue); the RSK breach case auto-opens with payout_hold. The D29 FAILED reversal restores the pre-breach state (FUNDED for funded accounts).

questions.question: docs/08 §3.3 bound V1 gap detection as per-login deal-ticket continuity (min(new) > last+1), but MT5 deal tickets are SERVER-GLOBAL counters — any other account on the server consumes tickets, so the check alarms on nearly every poll and EVL drowns in gap_flagged verdicts. Options — A: history-window count (deals in [last_synced_at−overlap, now] via history API vs rows written); B: defer gap detection to V2, V1 uses tick-staleness + nightly reconciliation only; C: keep the heuristic with a tuned threshold. See docs/51 §2 F1.
questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-19 — option A:** the V1 check is the history-window deals-count reconciliation; last_deal_ticket is a fetch cursor only, never a continuity oracle. The pf-platform scaffold's bridge-assigned per-account seq is the same lesson (ordering cursors must be ours, not the broker's).

questions.question: The D28 bridge.tick payload schema (5 fields) under-specified docs/08 §8's canonical shape (positions array, margin/free_margin, leverage, deals_count, last_deal_ticket), and §8 itself carried invalid JSON (leverage: 1:500). Which is canonical? Options — A: full §8 shape as the schema (fixing the JSON); B: minimal schema, consumers read PG. See docs/51 §2 F2.
questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-19 — option A:** the full §8 shape is the canonical payload schema (positions array for TD live view + RSK V2; leverage as a string); schema + example regenerated and strictly validated.

questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-20 — option A:** minimal V1 shapes for all three; docs/12 §9 + api/chk.md written.

questions.question: RELAY FAILOVER: the relay is exactly one instance (docs/01 §1.1: locked via PG advisory lock). What supervises it, how long is detection-to-restart, what happens to in-flight outbox rows, and what does a stalled relay do to notifications and tenant webhooks — or is this an accepted risk rather than a designed path? (Open since the 01 §1.1 'exactly one instance' note; the 04 §16 risk line only says 'outbox is durable + restart is the fix'.)
questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-20 — designed path, not accepted risk (full story in docs/06 §3.7).** Supervisor = compose `restart: always` on the prod box (compose IS the process supervisor there; the D56 standby host is a disaster standby, not an active HA pair — there is no second relay to fail over to) + the `relay:lock` PG advisory lock with a 30 s heartbeat steal (docs/04 §3.3) — a second/started relay cannot publish while the lock is held, and a dead one is stolen within 30 s. Detection = `relay.lag` Prometheus metric + CON gauge (docs/04 §11) and the `evt.relay_stopped` CRITICAL after 60 s without a publish (docs/04 §6 ext) + Uptime Kuma on `/readyz` (readyz already gates on relay lag < 60 s, docs/04 §4). Worst-case detection-to-restart ≈ 60–90 s. In-flight: nothing is in flight — rows leave the outbox only after the XADD batch succeeds (`published_at IS NULL` is the work queue, docs/04 §3.3); a relay that dies mid-run leaves rows in PG to be drained on restart, and at-least-once redelivery is absorbed by consumer idempotency on `event_id`. Exit criterion: kill relay 5 min → restart → zero lost, zero dupes (docs/04 §16 step 2). Backlog impact: notifications (NOT), tenant webhooks (Hook0 via consumers), LED postings, and ANA read models lag by the stall duration + drain time; the **trading path is unaffected** (bridge enforcement does not depend on events, docs/04 §16 risks). V2 candidate (not V1 scope): dual-relay lease handover for <30 s failover.

questions.question: STREAM RUNTIME: MetaApi's real-time account data (broker equity on every price packet, positions, deals) is only practically reachable through its streaming API, which MetaApi says to consume via its SDK (JS/Python/Java — no Go SDK). The bridge is Go (docs/01 §2 rejected Node for the hot sync path). How should the platform host the streaming client: a Node/TS sidecar on the official SDK, a Go port of the socket.io protocol, or a Java SDK sidecar?
questions.raised_by: Twenty-second pass — BRG streaming ingestion (2026-09-25, docs/63)
questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-25 — a thin Node/TS `bridge-stream` sidecar on the official `metaapi.cloud-sdk` (pinned 29.3.3).** The sidecar holds one SynchronizationListener per account and forwards ordered frames (Equity, AccountInfo, Positions, Deal, SyncState, Health, Downgrade) to the Go bridge over gRPC on a Unix socket. It does no money math (numbers cross as decimal strings; Go rounds per docs/09), holds no durable state (a PG-backed SDK HistoryStorage cursor lives in the bridge), makes no decisions, and reads equity only from raw packet values — never the SDK's local recompute (docs/63 F5). Recorded as ADR-15 (docs/01) — the one scoped exception to the Go-core rule. Rejected: a Go protocol port (we would own an evolving protocol MetaApi says not to re-implement); a Java sidecar (JVM on the single box + a third language). Licence = source-available, free for metaapi.cloud use → docs/34 review-before-deploy.

questions.question: INGEST MODE: docs/08 fixed V1 as poll-only every 60 s with streaming (BRG-21) in V3. MetaApi's documented CPU-credit limits (≈176 credits per account poll; 18k credits/min per front-end server) cap a 60-s poll at ≈100 accounts per server — V1's 431 accounts need ≥5 servers via client-id rotation, and V2's 10k accounts (≈1.76M credits/min) exceed all 12 servers combined (≈216k/min) ~8×; poll lag (≤60 s) is also enforcement lag. Streaming consumes no credits. Should V1 ingest move to streaming?
questions.raised_by: Twenty-second pass — BRG streaming ingestion (2026-09-25, docs/63)
questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-25 — streaming is the V1 primary ingest; REST polling is demoted to fallback + reconciliation.** BRG-21 is pulled forward from V3 to V1 (workbook unchanged; recorded in docs/08 §1 and docs/99). Accounts whose stream is `stale` > 30 s are REST-polled every 60 s under a per-client-id credit budget (≤80% of the per-server limit; funded/open-position accounts first); REST also serves the D33 history-window check at every (re)synchronization + hourly, BRG-09 on-demand refresh when the stream is not live, commands, and the nightly reconciler. Provisioning sets reliability (high for funded), region per broker group, riskManagementApiEnabled=false, metastatsApiEnabled=false; G2 required. Rejected: V1 poll-only with streaming in V2 (still needs client-id sharding, keeps 60-s lag); keep V3.

questions.question: HOT PATH: per-quote equity (≈3k frames/s at 10k accounts, 10k/s bursts) cannot ride the outbox (relay capacity 10k events/min; every event is kept 13 months). How do streamed updates reach EVL with minimum latency without breaking ADR-6 (transactional outbox) — conflate at the bridge and keep the outbox, grant an ADR-6 exception for a tick stream, or call EVL directly with async persistence?
questions.raised_by: Twenty-second pass — BRG streaming ingestion (2026-09-25, docs/63)
questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-25 — keep the transactional outbox; conflate at the bridge; group commit; NOTIFY doorbell.** The bridge holds per-account hot state and emits `bridge.tick` only on triggers: deal, position change (urgent), guard (equity within a guard band — default 50 bps of initial balance — of an EVL floor hint, ≤4/s; a floor crossing is never rate-capped, invariant I-21), material (abs Δequity ≥ 10 bps, ≤1/10 s), heartbeat (60 s open / 300 s flat, only while live), resync. A group-commit writer (≤25 ms / ≤500 rows; urgent = now) writes snapshots + deals + outbox + pg_notify('outbox_doorbell') in one tx; the relay LISTENs (1-s safety poll kept; NOTIFY is never transport). EVL returns advisory floor hints (evaluation_state.floor_daily/total/target + Redis `evl.floors`) — they change only when a tick is emitted, never what is decided. `bridge.tick` stays v1 with optional trigger/source/stream_seq/equity_low_cents/equity_high_cents (evidence; V1 rules still run at equity_cents). Envelope: V1 ≈10/s, V2 ≤250/s sustained, ≤1k/s burst (same order as the old poll plan); relay target raised to 60k events/min; platform-internal quote→verdict p95 < 50 ms. Correction: a relay stall pauses evaluation (docs/63 F6) — `bridge`-topic lag alert WARN 5 s / CRITICAL 30 s. Rejected: ADR-6 exception; direct bridge→EVL gRPC with async persistence.

questions.question: RISK-MANAGEMENT API: MetaApi's risk-management ('prop trading') API offers server-side drawdown/profit trackers with a resumable tracker-event stream, period statistics and equity charts. Should Alpha One use it — as a verdict source, as a watchdog, or not at all? (Tracker drawdown is measured against the period's initialBalance, has no trailing high-water mark, does not support MT5 netting, and is billed per account-hour on top of MetaApi; BVR-28 forbids vendor-final breaches.)
questions.raised_by: Twenty-second pass — BRG streaming ingestion (2026-09-25, docs/63)
questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-25 — optional V2 watchdog, off by default; never a verdict source.** When a tenant/program opts in, BRG mirrors the rule pack into trackers (daily loss → period 'date', total loss → 'lifetime' absolute threshold; trailing-HWM programs and netting accounts get none) and long-polls /users/current/tracker-events/stream with a PG-persisted previousSequenceNumber cursor. A tracker event on a live stream with no EVL breach within 30 s → `bridge.watchdog_divergence` (ext) → ADM review; on a stale stream → immediate BRG-09 REST refresh → urgent tick → EVL decides. Never touches LCC (BVR-28). EquityBalanceListener (a duplicate streaming connection), equity charts (ANA owns) and MetaStats/CopyFactory are not on the ingest path. Cost passed through (docs/22 §3.4).

questions.section: EVL state ownership — the stateless engine re-confirmed (twenty-third pass — docs/64 §4.1)
questions.question: STATE OWNERSHIP: the binding architecture assigns `evaluation_state`, per-account ordering, idempotency, retry and DLQ to a Go `workers` consumer (docs/63 §4.1's topology, docs/04 §3.5 + §13, docs/09 §2/§3.2), and ADR-11 says the Rust engine is stateless. But `propfirm-engine` has grown a tenant-scoped Postgres `AccountStore` with optimistic concurrency (1,838 lines, 9 migrations, its own `accounts`/`positions`/`trades`/`events` schema), its own `IdempotencyStore`, its own rule-pack lifecycle and service-bearer auth, and `/internal/v1/{evaluate,override,manual-run,emergency-stop}` endpoints that read and write account state directly — `/evaluate` loads the account from its own store instead of taking state in the request. Two components now both believe they own account state, and it was never decided either way. Options — A: pare the engine back to ADR-11's scope (a stateless compute service) and build the `workers` consumer on docs/04 §3.5's existing pattern; B: keep the self-contained engine and delete the planned `workers` evaluation consumer; C: write a bespoke Rust consumer for the `evaluation` lane only; D: keep both and reconcile with OCC. Which, and why — before the multi-tenant scale-up, because two owners of account state is a much worse problem at 100k accounts across 10 tenants than at 431?
questions.raised_by: Twenty-third pass — EVL state ownership + the multi-tenant capacity correction (2026-09-25, docs/64)
questions.deadline: Before the multi-tenant scale-up — docs/64 §6 step 1 (the `workers` consumer) must land before the engine is stripped
questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-25 — A. The Rust engine is pared back to ADR-11's original scope: a stateless compute service `evaluate(state, rules, tick) → (verdict, new_state, hints)`, with no database connection of its own, no tenant/account CRUD and no idempotency store. ADR-11 is re-confirmed and dated, not superseded.** State ownership, per-account/per-tenant ordering, retries and DLQ move to a `workers` evaluation consumer built on the platform's **existing** Go consumer-supervisor pattern (docs/04 §3.5: per-entity serial lanes via consistent hashing, `(event_id, consumer)` idempotency in `consumer_state`, `max_attempts: 5` with `1 s × 2^k`, `dlq.{consumer}` + the `relay dlq retry` path) — the same mechanism NOT/LED/AUD already use, not a new one invented for EVL. **Why, so this is not silently re-litigated:** (1) duplicating ordering/idempotency/retry semantics across two implementations is a maintenance *and correctness* liability that gets materially worse at white-label multi-tenant scale — every fix is made and tested twice and the two drift, as this review already found four times (an unconsulted `RulePackStore`, two idempotency semantics, a doc-comment contradicting its own function, generator drift); (2) a stateless compute tier is what makes horizontal scaling of the engine trivial — add replicas, no sharding logic of its own to get right — which matters directly at 100k+ accounts, whereas a stateful engine makes N replicas N competing writers on the same rows; (3) docs/09 §3.2's single-writer-per-account guarantee becomes **structural** rather than transactional, because OCC detects a violated invariant and the spec asks for one that cannot be violated. **Moves to `workers`:** the Postgres-backed `AccountStore` (reads/writes of `evaluation_state`), the idempotency store, per-account/tenant ordering, retry/DLQ, and the parts of `override`/`manual-run`/`emergency-stop` that mutate persisted account state (the *decision* of whether to allow an override stays engine logic; the *write* belongs in `workers`). **Stays in `propfirm-engine`:** the pure rule/decision math (`pure::evaluate`, everything under `rules/`, `engine/decision.rs`, `risk/`), the rule-pack schema/**validation** logic, the `EquityInput` provenance guard, the proptest + golden-replay corpus, and a narrow HTTP surface (`/evaluate`, plus new stateless `/rule-packs/validate` and `/explain`, plus the probes) — 14 routes reduced to 7, dispositioned case by case in docs/64 §4.3. Rule-pack **storage and lifecycle** (draft/active/superseded) move to where ADM's editor persists them, which resolves the long-standing 'RulePackStore isn't consulted during evaluation' gap **by removing the parallel-and-disconnected system rather than connecting it**. Rejected: B (contradicts docs/04 §3.5, docs/09 §2/§3.2 and docs/63 §4.1, forfeits the `consumer_state`/DLQ/replay tooling ops already uses, and leaves the engine owning a sharding problem at the scale where sharding mistakes are expensive); C (a *third* ordering/idempotency implementation, and it would put the money-loop lane outside `relay dlq …` and the CON DLQ screen); D (that is today's state, and findings G1–G4 are its output). **Blocker registered:** the `workers` evaluation consumer does not exist yet (`pf-platform/go/` has `gw/` and `bridge/` but no `workers/`), so the migration is consumer-first — stripping the engine before the consumer lands would leave the platform with no evaluation path at all (docs/64 §6). **Open item O-1, stated so it cannot hide behind a green build:** removing the disconnected store does *not* by itself make tenant-authored rule packs effective — `workers` must pass the bound `(rule_pack_id, version)` and `/evaluate` must build its registry from that document rather than the account's plan preset. Full text: docs/64.

questions.section: Per-tenant fairness on the event bus (twenty-third pass — docs/63 §4.13)
questions.question: TENANT FAIRNESS: at the corrected target (10 tenants × 10k accounts, docs/29 §1.1) nothing prevents one tenant's traffic spike from degrading another tenant's evaluation latency. Two mechanisms cause it: all tenants sharing one `topic.bridge` stream means one consumer group chews one FIFO (a tenant generating 80 % of ticks takes ≈ 80 % of consumer capacity), and `workers`' globally-hashed lanes mean a tenant's accounts share **serial** lanes with other tenants' accounts, so tenant A's backlog head-of-line-blocks tenant B's accounts on the same lane — invisible in aggregate throughput. Options — A: shard Redis Streams per tenant (separate stream keys, consumer groups per shard); B: shard per tenant-*tier*; C: per-tenant weighted fair queuing across `workers` lanes on a shared stream. Which?
questions.raised_by: Twenty-third pass — EVL state ownership + the multi-tenant capacity correction (2026-09-25, docs/64)
questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-25 — A. One Redis Stream per tenant (`topic.bridge.{tenant_id}`) with its own consumer group, plus `workers` lane sets owned by exactly one tenant shard.** Lane allocation is weighted with a floor: `max(10, ceil(weight_t × total))` per tenant, total `max(128, 10 × tenants)`, `weight_t` defaulting to the tenant's share of deployed accounts and CON-editable. **The floor of 10 lanes is that tenant's own burst design point** (10 lanes × ≈ 100 ticks/s = 1,000 ticks/s = docs/63 §4.4's per-tenant burst), so a tenant can absorb its own news burst without borrowing capacity it may not get back. The supervisor round-robins over tenant lane sets that have work; within a set, lanes stay serial per account (`hash(account_id) → lane`, docs/04 §3.5 unchanged). **Why sharding and not C (weighted fair queuing on a shared stream): C is not implementable on Redis Streams without sharding.** `XREADGROUP >` delivers undelivered entries in stream-id order to whichever consumer asks, so the consumer never chooses which tenant's work to take next — the stream decides. Exercising a choice requires either per-tenant streams or reading into a local buffer and reordering there, which abandons ADR-7's at-least-once-plus-idempotent simplicity and adds unbounded in-process buffering to a component whose job is to be restartable. Per-tenant streams are the *precondition* for any fairness policy; WFQ is then trivially expressible on top, which is what the lane weights implement. **B (tenant-tier) rejected** because it re-creates mechanism 1 inside a tier. One stream per tenant (rather than per tier) is affordable — 10 streams × `MAXLEN ~100k` × ≈ 1 KB ≈ 1 GB, inside `redis-streams`' 2 GB (D51); ≈ 5 GB at docs/00 §5's 50 tenants, so the D51 2/2/4 split becomes 2/6/4 — and it aligns the isolation unit with everything else already per tenant: docs/63 §4.2's shard ownership (the hash becomes `(tenant_id, account_id)`, 5 shards per tenant), §4.7's MetaApi credential set and credit budget, and docs/00 §8 #2. **One tenant = one shard set = one stream = one lane set = one credit budget.** The section also fixes the `MAXLEN ~100000` **trim hazard** the sharding exposes: a 5-minute fleet-wide burst puts ≈ 150k entries behind one tenant's group, past the trim point. Trimmed entries are not lost (the outbox + `events` log are the replay source, ADR-6/7) but silent trimming would be a silent evaluation gap, so the consumer compares `last-delivered-id` against `XINFO STREAM`'s `first-entry`/`max-deleted-entry-id`, emits **`evl.stream_trimmed`** and replays that tenant's range from PG; D84's shedding is the prevention. `MAXLEN` is deliberately **not** raised to ~1M (≈ 10 GB at 10 tenants) because Redis is never the source of truth (docs/00 §8 #1). DLQ stays single per consumer with `tenant_id` in the envelope and a per-tenant depth alert. Accepted by load test **LT-4/I-31**: with tenant A at 10× weight, tenants B–J's quote→verdict p95 is unchanged within measurement noise and no `evl.tick_stale` fires outside A. Full text: docs/63 §4.13.

questions.section: Postgres write scaling for `evaluation_state` at the corrected target (twenty-third pass — docs/29 §3.4)
questions.question: PG WRITE SCALING: at 100,000 accounts the evaluation path is ≈ 11.8k q/s sustained and ≈ 42.9k q/s burst (≈ 2.6k / ≈ 10.1k commits/s) against a single AX42-class primary planned at ≈ 10k q/s. A 5-minute burst at 10k ticks/s against a 5k ticks/s write path drains in exactly **10 minutes = the `evl.tick_stale` threshold**, i.e. zero margin against the correctness backstop. Options — A: partition by `tenant_id` and stay single-primary; B: adopt horizontal Postgres (Citus) now; C: shard by `account_id`; D: a second primary with per-tenant write routing; E: do nothing and rely on `evl.tick_stale`. Also: what is the read-replica story for ANA, disputes and ADM, and is single-primary-with-partitioning sufficient at this target or must the plan include a horizontal option?
questions.raised_by: Twenty-third pass — EVL state ownership + the multi-tenant capacity correction (2026-09-25, docs/64)
questions.deadline: Before the V2 second box is bought — the trigger is measured (docs/29 §1.1.1 trigger 6, load test LT-5)
questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-25 — A, with the horizontal option staged on a measured trigger rather than adopted or dismissed.** (1) **Partition `evaluation_state` by `tenant_id`** (hash, 64 buckets — covers docs/00 §5's 50-tenant range without re-partitioning, and a power of two so D82's shard mapping and the bucket mapping agree); every evaluation query is tenant-scoped by docs/00 §8 #2, so pruning applies to 100 % of the hot path. (2) **Partition `account_snapshots` and `broker_deals` by `(tenant_id, day)`** — their write volume *is* comparable (1,667/s and 58/s vs 2,500/s) and their row counts are far larger (≈ 2.0 B and ≈ 450 M in their rolling windows), so day partitioning turns retention into `DROP PARTITION` instead of a `DELETE` over billions of rows. (3) **Partition `events` by day** and give `bridge.tick` a **≤ 7-day hot window + R2 columnar archive** (docs/63 F13: 13 months (≈ 395 d) at 2,500/s is ≈ 85 B rows ≈ 34 TB vs docs/29 §1.3's '≈ 200 GB/yr, 1 TB disk' — ≈ 605 GB hot and ≈ 3 TB/yr ≈ $45/mo archived instead). Every other topic keeps the 13-month PG window; they are 3–4 orders of magnitude smaller. (4) **One write path per account, structurally** — D81 + D82 together are what make docs/09 §3.2's single-writer guarantee real; before D81 the engine's OCC `AccountStore` was a second writer and OCC turned a correctness property into a retry loop. **Read-replica story: nothing outside the evaluation write path reads the primary.** `workers` (the lane's state read+write), the bridge's floor-hint reload on cache miss, and PAY eligibility (BRG-09 — a payout decision must not read a lagging replica) stay on the primary; ANA's read model, dispute replay, ADM/TD screens and RSK's batch detectors read the replica under the `_ro` role, and dispute replay older than the F13 hot window reads the R2 archive rather than PG at all. Replication is physical streaming (docs/06 §3.3's failover strategy extended, doing double duty as the read scale-out and the D56 warm-standby promotion path), lag WARN 10 s / CRITICAL 60 s, and every human-visible replica read carries `as_of` so lag is disclosed (ANA-14). The replica lives on box 2, which is a **V2 prerequisite** (docs/63 F12) and carries `bridge-stream` shards *and* the replica — complementary loads (RSS-heavy + read-heavy) rather than two writers. **Is single-primary-with-partitioning sufficient? Sustained: yes** (≈ 11.8k q/s, ≈ 2.6k commits/s against a ≈ 10k-commit/s NVMe ceiling ⇒ ~4× commit headroom, ~1.2× CPU headroom). **Burst: no** — but burst need not be served at line rate, only drained inside the staleness window, and the drain arithmetic lands at exactly 10 minutes = the `evl.tick_stale` threshold, i.e. **zero margin**. That is why D84's shedding ladder exists (it removes ≈ 14 % of sustained load at level 1, ≈ 30 % at level 2 and ≈ 60 % at level 3, for zero correctness cost at levels 1–2, because it widens the conflation window rather than dropping observations — `equity_low/high_cents` still bound the gap, I-22) and why the horizontal option is staged rather than dismissed: **adopt Citus (distribution key `tenant_id`) when the load test or production shows sustained commits > 6,000/s (60 % of the ceiling, docs/29 §1.2's 2× rule applied to commits) for 2 weeks, or `evl_lag_seconds > 300` more than twice a month with the engine tier demonstrably unsaturated.** Not adopted now because the sustained load does not require it, because shedding is ~200 lines in a component that already exists while Citus is a new database topology, because Citus conflicts with docs/00 §8 #6 (operable by a 1-person DevOps team), and because ADR-6's outbox is a single-database transaction that would become a distributed one (solvable by co-locating a tenant's outbox with its evaluation rows under the same distribution key, but it must be designed, not discovered during an incident). **Partitioning first is not a dead end: `tenant_id` hash partitioning and a Citus `tenant_id` distribution key are the same sharding function, so the migration is a shard move, not a data-model change.** Rejected: C (sharding by `account_id` breaks tenant locality and docs/00 §8 #2); D (two write paths turn the single-writer guarantee into a coordination problem); E (`evl.tick_stale` is a correctness backstop, not a capacity plan — reaching it on funded accounts is already a docs/29 §4 SLO failure). **All throughput figures are planning estimates derived from documented per-unit limits, not measurements**; load test LT-5 retires them. Full text and the per-writer table: docs/29 §3.4.

questions.section: Autoscaling signal and load-shedding for the stateless engine tier (twenty-third pass — docs/63 §4.14)
questions.question: CAPACITY CONTROL: once D81 makes the engine genuinely stateless, what is the autoscaling signal, and what happens when lag outpaces scaling? `evl.tick_stale` (implemented, 10-minute threshold) stops verdicts on stale equity and is the correctness backstop — but it is not a capacity plan. What lag threshold pages someone, what is allowed to degrade gracefully, and what counts as an incident? Note the deployment target is Docker Compose on Hetzner (ADR-9) with no Kubernetes (docs/00 §8 #6), so there is no autoscaler to wire a metric to.
questions.raised_by: Twenty-third pass — EVL state ownership + the multi-tenant capacity correction (2026-09-25, docs/64)
questions.deadline: With the `workers` evaluation consumer (docs/64 §6 step 5); thresholds confirmed by load test LT-6
questions.answer: **Answered 2026-09-25 — Redis Streams consumer-group lag expressed as *time-to-drain*, acted on by an operator in V2, with load-shedding that widens the conflation window rather than dropping observations.** **The honest constraint first: the deployment target has no autoscaler.** ADR-9 is Compose on one Hetzner box and docs/00 §8 #6 forbids Kubernetes; Compose has `--scale` but no controller. So the story is stated for the platform that exists: in **V2** the signal is scraped by Prometheus and acted on by an **operator** (`docker compose up -d --scale engine=N --scale workers=M`, a runbook line, surfaced in CON); in **V2.5** — *only if the load test proves the manual loop too slow* — a ~200-line Compose-scale actuator reads the same metric within min/max bounds (explicitly optional, explicitly a new deployable, justified by measured operator response time before it is built); in **V3** the same metric feeds KEDA/HPA, which is why it is defined in lag terms rather than CPU. **The signal is lag in seconds, not entries**, because that is the quantity comparable to the correctness backstop: `evl_lag_seconds{tenant,group} = lag_entries ÷ measured_drain_rate`, `lag_entries` from `XINFO GROUPS → lag` (Redis ≥ 7.0), `measured_drain_rate` an EWMA of acknowledged entries/s over 60 s per group. Supporting metrics: `evl_stream_lag_entries`, `evl_lane_queue_depth{tenant,lane}`, `evl_evaluate_seconds` (the engine HTTP call — the stateless tier's own saturation), `evl_pg_state_seconds` (the shared resource), `evl_shed_level{tenant}`, `evl_stream_trimmed_total{tenant}`. **Engine CPU is deliberately not the scaling signal:** `propfirm-engine`'s `benches/engine.rs` measures ≈ 52,600 pure evals/s single-threaded (≈ 205k/s batched), so at a 10k verdict/s target the engine is never the bottleneck — HTTP fan-in and Postgres are, and scaling on engine CPU would add replicas to a tier that is not saturated while the real constraint goes unaddressed. **Thresholds are fractions of the 10-minute `evl.tick_stale` window (docs/09 §6), not chosen arbitrarily:** scale out at > 60 s for 60 s; **WARN** at > 120 s for 5 min (⇒ shed level 1, no page); **PAGE (P1) at > 300 s for 60 s** — half the window, i.e. verdicts begin being suppressed in ≈ 5 min if nothing changes; **INCIDENT** at > 480 s, or on any `evl.stream_trimmed`, or on any `evl.tick_stale` suppression on a **funded** account — declared, tenant-visible via CON-15, with the docs/29 §4 breach-to-enforcement SLO *formally suspended* for the duration and the suspension recorded; scale in below 30 s for 10 min. **What degrades gracefully: shedding raises the bridge conflator's thresholds — the same mechanism D79 already uses, not a new one — so a shed tick is not a lost observation, because `equity_low_cents`/`equity_high_cents` keep bounding what happened between emitted ticks (invariant I-22).** Level 1 (`heartbeat` 60 s → 180 s open / 300 s → 900 s flat, **non-funded accounts only**) takes the non-funded heartbeat term from 367/s to 122/s = **≈ 14 % of the ≈ 1,791/s sustained fleet rate, for zero correctness cost**; level 2 (+ `material` 10 bps → 25 bps for non-funded) is cumulative **≈ 30 %**; level 3 (+ funded heartbeats widen too **except guard-band accounts**, `material` widened fleet-wide, non-funded lane weight to the floor) is cumulative **≈ 60 %** — the ceiling is ≈ 60 % and not 100 % because funded accounts are half the fleet and the priority list protects them. Levels 1–2 cost nothing because heartbeats carry no new information (they only bound the stale-floor-hint worst case, ≤ 60 s → ≤ 180 s for non-funded) and **widening the interval cannot trip `evl.tick_stale`**, which measures tick *age* — `now − occurred_at`, the receive time of the newest frame folded in, including the `Health` frames arriving at ≤ 1 per 10 s while `live` — not emission cadence; a heartbeat never refreshes stale data and a `stale` stream emits none at all (docs/09 §6). Level 2 adds `material` 10 bps → 25 bps for non-funded accounts. Level 3 (the incident level) drops non-funded challenge accounts' lane weight to the floor while funded and guard-band accounts keep full rate. **The ordering reuses docs/63 §4.7's existing resync priority list (guard-band → funded → open positions → the rest) rather than inventing a new one.** **Never shed:** `deal`, `position`, `guard`, `guard`-crossing (I-21 — a crossing quote is never conflated away) and `resync` — the triggers that can change a verdict. **Delivery reuses the `evl.floors` pattern:** `workers` publishes `evl.load_shed {tenant_id, level, reason, at}` on Redis pub/sub and the bridge applies it, so the decision is made where lag is observable and the act happens where the tick is born (no outbox row, relay `XADD` or PG write is spent on a tick about to be deferred); Redis-down degrades to level 0 at the bridge — the safe direction — with the same 30 s PG-reload fallback floor hints use. **`evl.tick_stale` is explicitly not a capacity plan:** a system that reaches it on funded accounts has already failed its docs/29 §4 SLO, which is why that condition is an incident and not a degradation. Accepted by load tests **LT-6/I-30** (the ladder removes ≈ 14 % / ≈ 30 % / ≈ 60 % at levels 1/2/3 as predicted; zero `deal`/`position`/`guard`/crossing/`resync` ticks shed at any level; I-22 holds across every widened window) and LT-7 (the trim hazard).
